Claims about what materials DOJ sought, threats of contempt or a direct connection to particular White House complaints require additional reporting or court records.

proposal.title: SSA Reports a Falling Disability Claims Backlog
proposal.description_short: SSA reported that pending initial disability claims fell 25% to 940,000 by July 23, 2025.
proposal.description_medium: On July 23, 2025, the Social Security Administration said its initial disability claims backlog had fallen to 940,000 pending cases, 25 percent below a record of more than 1.2 million the previous year. The agency also reported shorter phone, field-office and disability-hearing waits. These are SSA-reported service figures; they do not establish that millions faced new delays after July staff cuts.
proposal.description_long: On July 23, 2025, the Social Security Administration reported that its initial disability claims backlog had fallen to 940,000 pending cases. SSA said this was a 25 percent reduction from a record of more than 1.2 million cases the previous year. The agency attributed service changes to new telephone technology, process engineering and resource alignment. It also reported faster customer service: its National 800 Number handled nearly 1.3 million calls the prior week, 70 percent more than in the comparable week a year earlier, while the average wait to speak with an agent was six minutes. SSA said field office wait times averaged 23 minutes so far that year, compared with 30 minutes in the prior year. The release further reported that the number of pending disability hearings remained at historic lows and average hearing waits had fallen by 60 days since June 2024. These are agency-reported service figures and do not establish the separate claim that millions newly faced crippling delays after July DOGE cuts. The narrow event supported here is SSA’s July 23 public report on service performance and backlog reduction.

supports: SSA reported 940,000 pending initial disability claims, 25% below a prior-year record above 1.2 million.
SSA reported service and hearing wait improvements; this does not prove millions were newly delayed after July cuts.

proposal.title: BLS Reports August 2025 CPI Rose 2.9% Over the Year
proposal.description_short: BLS reported August 2025 CPI rose 0.4% monthly and 2.9% over 12 months.
proposal.description_medium: On September 11, 2025, BLS reported that the Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers rose 0.4 percent in August and 2.9 percent over the 12 months ending that month. Shelter was the largest contributor to the monthly increase; food rose 0.5 percent and energy 0.7 percent. The release does not support the original 6 percent figure or establish that tariffs caused the change.
proposal.description_long: On September 11, 2025, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Consumer Price Index for August. The CPI for All Urban Consumers increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis during the month, following a 0.2 percent increase in July. Over the 12 months ending in August, the all-items index rose 2.9 percent before seasonal adjustment. The shelter index rose 0.4 percent and was the largest factor in the monthly increase; food rose 0.5 percent and energy rose 0.7 percent. The index for all items less food and energy increased 0.3 percent in August and 3.1 percent over 12 months. BLS also reported gasoline prices rose 1.9 percent in the month. The official release therefore contradicts the entry’s claim that consumer prices surged 6 percent in August. The event can be retained as a dated statistical release, while any claim about tariff effects requires separate evidence and should not be conflated with the aggregate CPI result.

supports: BLS reported August CPI-U rose 0.4% monthly and 2.9% over 12 months, with the listed component changes.
The official numbers contradict the frozen 6% claim; this release alone does not establish tariff causation.

proposal.description_short: On June 9, 2017, New York’s attorney general said the office was looking into issues raised about the Eric Trump Foundation.

proposal.description_long: On June 9, 2017, the New York Attorney General’s office said it was looking into issues raised by a report about the Eric Trump Foundation. ABC News reported that questions concerned the charity’s annual golf fundraiser and payments involving Trump Organization golf properties. Eric Trump’s spokesperson said the foundation would cooperate with the office. The foundation had announced in December 2016 that it would cease direct fundraising; Eric Trump cited his father’s election and the transition to the presidency. The foundation’s fundraising remained suspended during the subsequent review, and contemporaneous reporting said the state attorney general’s office had previously issued a notice of violation. The June statement was the office’s public response to questions about the charity and did not announce a new fundraising suspension. The available accounts describe a review announcement, not an adjudication, criminal charge, or determination that funds were misused.

supports: The AG office said June 9, 2017 it was looking into issues; the statement was not an adjudication.
